hints: Focus on what must happen to the R-X molecule before any silver halide cloudiness can appear.
Compare the C-Cl, C-Br and C-I bonds, the larger halogen gives a longer and weaker bond that is easier to break.
Connect bond strength to activation energy, the weakest bond breaks fastest and so gives precipitate fastest.
walkthrough:
**See what the cloudiness tells you**

Think of the cloudiness as the signal that hydrolysis has happened. The faster the $R-X$ hydrolyses to give $X^-(aq)$, the faster $AgX(s)$ precipitates.

$$H_2O(l) + R-X(l) + Ag^+(aq) \rightarrow R-OH(aq) + AgX(s) + H^+(aq)$$

**Find the slow, bond-breaking step**

For hydrolysis, the $C-X$ bond must break to release the halide ion. Breaking a stronger bond needs more energy and has a higher activation energy, so it is slower.

**Apply the bond energy trend**

Bond length increases and bond strength decreases down Group 17. So bond energy is in the order $C-Cl > C-Br > C-I$.

That means $R-I$ breaks most easily and reacts fastest, giving $RCl < RBr < RI$ for rate of cloudiness.

options.A: Correct. The rate is controlled by how easily the C-X bond breaks. Bond energy falls from RCl to RI because the bond gets longer and weaker, so RI hydrolyses fastest and gives AgI precipitate fastest.
options.B: Not correct. First ionisation energy refers to forming $X^+(g)$ from $X(g)$, but this reaction forms $X^-(aq)$ by breaking C-X. It is a common trap to link any Group 17 trend to reactivity, but ionisation is not involved here.
options.C: Not correct. It is true that AgI is less soluble than AgCl, but all three silver halides are very insoluble and precipitate readily. Solubility affects how much stays dissolved, not how fast the R-X bond breaks and supplies halide ions.
options.D: Not correct. Bond polarity does decrease from RCl to RI because electronegativity difference gets smaller. If polarity controlled the rate, RCl would be fastest, which is the opposite of what is observed. Strength, not polarity, is decisive.
